subject: Cognitive Science
title: Prediction in Reading
description: A quick win: understand Prediction in Reading.

hook.text: 'She spread the warm bread with...' Your brain already expects 'butter' before your eyes reach it.

buildup.text: Brain wave studies show that predicted words trigger less neural activity. The brain pre-activates them.

discovery.text: The N400—a brain signal for semantic surprise—is large for unexpected words and tiny for predicted ones.

twist.text: Even the word's phonology is predicted. An unexpected word starting with the wrong sound triggers extra processing.

climax.text: Reading isn't just decoding—it's constant guessing. Your brain runs a prediction engine under every sentence.

punchline.text: You've read the next word before you see it.

quiz.question: What does the N400 brain signal measure?

details.summary: Readers predict upcoming words before they appear. When predictions are confirmed, reading speeds up. When violated, processing slows. Predictable words are fixated for less time and sometimes skipped entirely. The brain generates expectations at every level: phonological, syntactic, and semantic.
details.whyItMatters: Prediction makes reading fast and efficient. Understanding predictive processing explains both fluent reading and the difficulties of reading in a foreign language.
takeaways: Readers generate expectations about upcoming words
Confirmed predictions speed up processing; violations slow it
Prediction operates at sound, grammar, and meaning levels

faq.question: How do we know readers predict words?
faq.answer: Cloze tasks show readers can guess words from context. Eye-tracking shows predictable words receive shorter fixations or are skipped. EEG reveals a smaller N400 brainwave for predicted words, indicating less processing effort. The converging evidence from behavior, eyes, and brain signals is strong.

faq.question: Do skilled and poor readers predict differently?
faq.answer: Skilled readers are better predictors, using context more effectively to anticipate upcoming content. Poor readers rely more on laborious word-by-word decoding.
